title: Real Zombie Animals: Parasites That Hijack Brains. #1 Is in You
description: Zombies are real, and they're tiny. From a snail with pulsing eyes to wolves turned into pack leaders, here are 5 parasites that hijack animals from the inside. Number one may be living in one in three people. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.
sources: Deans, T. scenes.say: This cockroach isn't dead, but its brain actually belongs to someone else.
Something took over its brain. And it's not a movie monster. It's a tiny wasp, smaller than your thumb.
scenes.label: Real zombie maker

scenes.say: Happy Halloween, by the way. Because today we're talking about real zombies. Animals that get hijacked from the inside.
Five of them, from creepy to completely unbelievable. And number one? Number one might be inside you right now.
scenes.label: Stay for #1

scenes.say: Scientists think about one in three people on Earth carry it. Yeah. We'll get there. Stay till the end.
Okay, so first, a quick question for you. If a parasite controlled your body, would you even notice? Keep that in mind.
Let's start with a snail that looks like it's wearing two glowing caterpillars on its face.
scenes.label: Zombie snail

scenes.say: Those aren't its eyes. They're swollen tubes stuffed with baby flatworms. And they pulse. In the light, they throb like a heartbeat.
Here's the thing. A snail wants to hide. Dark, damp, low to the ground, away from hungry birds.
Infected snails do the opposite. In a 2013 study in a Polish forest, they sat higher up, in brighter, more open spots.
scenes.label: 2013 study

scenes.say: They also wandered around more, on weird, zig-zag paths. Basically, they became a walking advertisement.
Advertising to who? To birds. The worm needs a bird's gut to finish growing up. The snail is just the delivery van.
The bird eats the pulsing tube, the worm grows inside the bird, and its eggs drop out in bird poop.
Then a new snail eats that poop. And the whole creepy loop starts again. People first described this way back in 1835.
scenes.label: Known since 1835

scenes.say: Creepy, right? But the snail at least stays on land. The next zombie gets marched straight into the water.
Number four is a cricket that walks to a stream and jumps in. Crickets can't swim. It does it anyway.
scenes.label: Suicide jump?

scenes.say: Inside it is a hairworm. A long, thin worm coiled up inside the cricket's body, like spaghetti in a bag.
scenes.label: Hairworm

scenes.say: The worm grows on land, but it can only mate in water. So when it's ready, it needs its ride to go swimming.
And it works on praying mantises too. In one outdoor test, 14 of 16 infected mantises that jumped picked the pool reflecting a special kind of light.
scenes.label: 14 out of 16

scenes.say: That light is horizontally polarized. It's the kind of shine water gives off. So the worm may be making its host chase the look of water.
The cricket splashes in, and the worm wriggles out into the stream. Mission complete.
Imagine a worm coiled up inside you, quietly steering where you walk. For that cricket, this is real life. It never even knew.
But here's the twist. In Japan, scientists found infected crickets were 20 times more likely to end up in streams.
scenes.label: 20x more likely

scenes.say: And trout were waiting. Crickets and grasshoppers made up about 60 percent of the trout's energy for the whole year.
scenes.label: 60% of the food

scenes.say: Think about that. A tiny worm, controlling crickets, is basically feeding an endangered fish. One parasite is running a whole river's menu.
So far, the hijackers are hiding inside. But number three does it from the outside. With surgery.
Remember our cockroach from the start? Meet the jewel wasp. Shiny, metallic green, and terrifyingly precise.
scenes.label: Jewel wasp

scenes.say: First sting goes into the roach's chest. That freezes its front legs for a few minutes, so it can't fight back.
Second sting goes into the head. Right into the brain. The stinger is only about 2 millimeters long.
scenes.label: 2 mm stinger

scenes.say: And the wasp spends about a minute feeling around in there, searching for exactly the right spot. Like a surgeon.
The venom hits the part of the brain that starts movement. The roach can still walk. It just doesn't want to go anywhere on its own.
So the wasp grabs it by one antenna and walks it home. Like a dog on a leash.
scenes.label: Roach on a leash

scenes.say: Here's what makes it wild. The roach is way bigger than the wasp. It could run. It just... doesn't.
Inside the burrow, the wasp lays an egg on it. Over several days, the larva eats the roach, then comes out as an adult about a month later.
Okay, quick break. If you're enjoying this, subscribe for one animal secret a day. Because number two is the famous one. And it's way weirder than the rumors.
Number two. The zombie ant fungus. This is the real-life inspiration behind a lot of zombie stories.
scenes.label: Zombie ant fungus

scenes.say: It starts with one spore landing on an ant. It sticks, breaks through the shell, and starts growing inside.
In Thailand, scientists found it takes about 3 to 9 days to turn the ant into a full zombie.
scenes.label: 3 to 9 days

scenes.say: The ant leaves its colony. It starts walking strangely and having convulsions. It even falls off its tree.
Then it climbs a plant to about 25 centimeters above the ground. Not 10. Not 50. About 25.
scenes.label: 25 cm high

scenes.say: Most of the dead ants were found where humidity was about 95 percent, and temperatures ran about 20 to 30 degrees Celsius.
scenes.label: 95% humidity

scenes.say: And the final bite usually happens around solar noon. The ant clamps onto a leaf vein and locks its jaws. The death grip.
scenes.label: Death grip at noon

scenes.say: After it dies, a stalk grows out of its head and rains spores onto the ants walking below. The whole thing takes about two to three weeks.
Why so picky? Down in the understory, the air is cooler and wetter. Perfect for the fungus to grow. So the ant dies exactly where the fungus needs it.
But here's the part most people get wrong. The fungus doesn't actually eat the brain.
Researchers found the fungus wrapped all through the body and around the muscles. But not inside the brain.
scenes.label: Brain left alone

scenes.say: So the ant's brain may still be there, while the fungus works its body like a puppet. Honestly, that's even creepier.
And twist number two. This year, scientists in Borneo found a new fungus that attacks the zombie fungus itself.
scenes.label: New in 2026

scenes.say: They named it Pleurocordyceps cornusynnemata. It feeds right on the zombie fungus inside the dead ant. The hunter gets hunted.
And now, number one. A single-celled parasite called Toxoplasma. And it can only finish its life cycle inside a cat.
scenes.label: Toxoplasma

scenes.say: So what does it do to a rat? Normally, a rat smells cat and runs. Infected rats can lose that fear. Some even seem attracted to it.
The rat walks toward the cat. The cat eats the rat. The parasite gets home. Pretty neat trick for something you can't even see.
scenes.label: Back to the cat

scenes.say: But it doesn't stop at rats. In Gabon, scientists tested 33 chimpanzees. Nine of them were infected.
scenes.label: 33 chimps

scenes.say: They put leopard urine near the enclosures. Leopards hunt chimps in the wild. And the infected chimps checked it out more often.
Lion urine? Tiger urine? No difference. Only leopard. The one predator that actually eats chimps.
And here's the big one. In Yellowstone, scientists followed 229 wolves using 26 years of data.
scenes.label: 26 years of data

scenes.say: Infected wolves were 11 times more likely to leave their pack and go out alone. That's a bold move for a wolf.
scenes.label: 11x more likely

scenes.say: And they were about 46 times more likely to become pack leaders. A parasite might help decide who's boss.
scenes.label: 46x more likely

scenes.say: Where did the wolves catch it? Infection was highest where their land overlapped with cougars. Big cats, again.
Now the scary part. Scientists estimate about one in three people worldwide carry Toxoplasma too.
scenes.label: 1 in 3 people

scenes.say: Does it change us? Scientists are still arguing about that. Some studies suggest slower reaction times. Others find much less.
So remember that question from the start? If a parasite was steering you, would you even notice?
Which zombie freaked you out the most? The snail, the cricket, the roach, the ant, or the wolf? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: This Zombie Ant Still Has Its Brain
short.description: A fungus turns ants into zombies, makes them bite a leaf at noon, then grows out of their heads. The surprise: it leaves the brain alone. Full countdown of 5 real zombie animals on my channel.

scenes.say: This ant is a zombie, and its brain is actually still there.
A fungus spore lands on it, breaks through the shell, and grows all through its body. In 3 to 9 days, it takes over.
The ant leaves its colony, climbs about 25 centimeters up a plant, and around noon, bites a leaf and locks its jaws.
Then a stalk grows out of its head and rains spores on ants below.
But here's the creepy part. Scientists found the fungus wrapped around its muscles, not inside its brain.
So it may be working the ant's body like a puppet. And this year, scientists found a new fungus that hunts the zombie fungus.
So next time you see an ant stuck on a leaf, look closer. This ant is a zombie, and its brain is actually still there.
